newsitem.title: USA: Big foreign wheat crops to cut U.S. exports -- trade.
newsitem.headline: Big foreign wheat crops to cut U.S. exports -- trade.

text.p: Expected record wheat crops from Argentina and Australia are expected to divert most export business away from U.S. markets in the coming months, grain exporters and analysts said.
"I'd be very surprised if we (the U.S.) get any business of consequence any time soon," said an exporter in the U.S. Pacific Northwest.

Record crops from Australia and Argentina should pressure world wheat prices. Final crop estimates for those countries keep creeping higher, and the bulk of the crops are expected to end up on the world market, analysts and traders said.

"It is my understanding that they (Argentina and Australia) don't have as adequate storage facilities as we do, so it (wheat) has to be sold," said Joel Karlin, grains analyst with Everen Securities brokerage in Chicago.
The competing countries will have to discount wheat sharply in order to sell it, so those prices will most likely stay $10 to $15 per tonne below U.S. wheat prices, Karlin said.
Private estimates for the Australian wheat crop have come in as high as 24 million tonnes, and Argentine forecasts have climbed as high as 16 million, sources said.
In its January world crop forecast, the U.S. Department of Agriculture put the 1996/97 Australian wheat crop at 21.5 million tonnes, and the agency estimated Argentina's crop at 15.5 million.
The U.S. export outlook will only darken when U.S. wheat crops are harvested in the summer and supplies grow even larger, one wheat exporter said.
"Come this summer, everybody is going to have plenty of wheat to sell," the exporter said. "We might even see the EEP (Export Enhancement) program come back to life."
Others characterized the revival of the EEP subsidy program as unlikely because there is little money allocated for the program this year. Currently, there is $100 million allocated in EEP.
"It would be very difficult to get back into EEP," Karlin said. "We'd have to get more funding, and from what I understand, that would be very difficult."
In recent export news, most business went to France and Australia. Iraq bought between 250,000 and 275,000 tonnes of French wheat for March and April delivery.
Additionally, Australian Wheat Board officials said this week that they expected to sell another 100,000 tonnes of wheat to Iraq under that country's food-for-oil program.
